What one kind of element is: its tag, the properties it can carry, whether it holds children, and the styles it starts with before any class list touches it. One instance of each is registered in `ElementRegistry`, and the parser makes a fresh one per element it reads.

An element's styles are three layers: the plain classes under every layer of classes whose variants are holding, under whatever was set by hand. Reading the class property again replaces everything the classes said before it, which is what lets a callback show a box it had hidden.

Adding an element of your own is a subclass that calls this constructor with its tag, and overrides `defaultStyle` where it behaves differently from a plain div.

```java
import net.tutla.craftytml.client.ctml.CTMLElement;
```

### `public static final ElementStyle DEFAULTS`

Where an element starts before any class or hand set style lands on it, which is what css calls the initial values. Only the non inherited ones belong here: putting a text colour on every element would stop the parent's colour ever reaching the child.

### `public static final ElementStyle INHERITED_INITIAL`

The initial values of the styles that come down the tree, which belong to nothing in particular: putting them on an element as a default would stop the parent's value ever reaching it. They are seeded once at the root of whatever is being laid out instead, so the tree bottoms out in them however it is rooted, with or without a `<ctml>` over it.

### `public ElementStyle defaultStyle()`

Overridden by the elements that behave differently from a plain div.

### `public void applyClassStyles(String classList)`

### `public void applyClassStyles(String classList, TusanContext ctx)`

Reads a class list onto the element, and says so about every class it could not use: one nothing knows at all, and one whose value is no use to the style it names. Neither stops the screen being built, since a single typo should cost one class and not the whole file.

### `public ElementStyle getStyle()`

Everything set on the element, with its own defaults underneath for whatever is left.

### `public ElementStyle getOwnStyle()`

Only what was actually set on this element, so defaults don't get mistaken for author styles.

### `public boolean setHovered(boolean hovered)`

Whether the cursor is over the element or over something inside it, which is what hover: asks. Said by whatever is watching the cursor, and only worth anything where a class asked about it: the answer is kept either way, and the tree is only marked as changed where it moves something.

### `public boolean setFocused(boolean focused)`

Whether the element itself has the keyboard, behind focus: and focus-visible:.

### `public boolean setFocusWithin(boolean focusWithin)`

Whether something inside the element has it, which only focus-within: asks about.

### `public boolean setActive(boolean active)`

Whether a button is being held on the element or on something inside it, behind active:.

### `public int getTabIndex()`

Where the element comes in the tab order, or TabIndex.UNSET where it says nothing. Something that says nothing can still be focused if it scrolls, which is the one thing the keyboard can do to it.

### `public int defaultTabIndex()`

Where the element sits in the tab order when the script says nothing, which for everything but a button is nowhere. A browser has the same idea: a div is not tabbable and a button always is.

### `public boolean firesInput()`

Whether a press on it is an input rather than a plain click. True for the things a user operates.

### `public String getId()`

The id on the element: the one the script gave it, or one made up here the first time it is asked for. Made up ids are handed out in order and never land on one a script wrote, so every element in a tree can be named whether or not anyone bothered to name it.

### `public String getCallback()`

The callback named on the element, or null where it names none.

### `public int getDragX(){ return dragX; }`

### `public int getDragY(){ return dragY; }`

### `public void setDragOffset(int dragX, int dragY)`

Straight pixels, which is all a script has to go on, so this forgets any share that was remembered. Whatever lays the element out works a share back out from it once it knows the room it had.

### `public void setDragShare(float shareX, float shareY)`

How far along the room it was allowed the element was put, from nothing to all of it. That is what gets remembered, so a window resize or a gui scale change brings the element back to the spot it was put rather than to the same number of pixels. Below zero means nothing is remembered.

### `public float getDragShareX(){ return dragShareX; }`

### `public float getDragShareY(){ return dragShareY; }`

### `public boolean isDragged()`

Whether the element has been dragged at all, which a share of zero still counts as.

### `public void setContext(DOMContext context)`

Told to the element by the context it ends up in, which is where its strings look their ${variables} up. An element that is in none reads its strings exactly as they were written.

### `public DOMContext getContext()`

### `public String resolve(String raw)`

A string as the screen shows it, with every ${variable} in it filled in.

### `public String getStringProperty(String name)`

A string property as the screen shows it: the value with its ${variables} filled in, or null where nothing set it. Every string the element is read for comes through here, bar the id, which is the one string that has to stay what it was: it is what the element is found by.

### `public void rereadVariables()`

Said to the element when a variable changed: anything of its own naming one is out of date, and a class list naming one has to be read on again, since classes are parsed as they are set.

A scroll a script asked for, which slides where the style says to: css lets scroll-behavior have its say over the scrolls that are asked for, whatever it does about the wheel and the keys.

### `public boolean isSliding()`

Whether the content is still on its way somewhere, which is what keeps the frames coming.

### `public boolean advanceScroll(float seconds, float tau)`

Moves the content a share of the way left to go, which over a few frames is an ease out. Always worth at least a pixel, so a slide with a long way to go cannot stall just short.

### `public int scrollFor(boolean vertical, int max, long view)`

What layout should scroll the content by, given the room there turns out to be. A viewport that has changed since the pixels were written down goes back to the share instead, so a window resize or a gui scale change leaves the content looking at the same place rather than the same pixel.

### `public void settleScroll(int scrollX, int scrollY, int maxX, int maxY, long view)`

Told to the element once layout has worked out where the content ended up and how far it could go.
